title: I just took the train under Denver Airport and the engineering is actually incredible — here's what's really down there
content:
So I had a 4-hour layover at DEN last week and I went full nerd mode learning about the underground system. Turns out the tunnels under Denver Airport are honestly a really cool piece of engineering that gets totally overshadowed by all the conspiracy stuff.

The automated underground train system connects all three concourses and the main terminal. It moves something like 30 million passengers a year. Below that, there's an absolutely massive automated baggage handling system — when the airport opened in 1995 it was supposed to be the most advanced baggage system in the world. Key word: supposed to. It was actually a legendary disaster. The system kept shredding luggage and throwing bags everywhere. They spent $560 million on it before scrapping the automated part and going back to manual carts. It's actually a famous case study in engineering schools now about overcomplicating things.

The tunnels themselves were built as part of the original construction. DIA was built on 53 square miles of empty plains east of Denver — basically they built an entire small city from scratch. The amount of earth moved during construction was enormous, something like 110 million cubic yards, and yeah, that created a lot of underground space. But it's mostly just... infrastructure. Baggage tunnels. The train. Utility corridors. Electrical and HVAC systems.

The murals everyone freaks out about? They're by an artist named Leo Tanguma and they depict environmental destruction followed by peace and renewal. That's literally it. He's talked about them extensively. But I get it — a giant painting of a gas-mask soldier with a sword in an airport is a CHOICE and whoever approved that for an airport terminal deserves some side-eye lol.

Also the giant blue horse statue with glowing red eyes (locals call it Blucifer) actually killed its creator — a piece of it fell on the artist Luis Jimenez during construction. That part is genuinely dark but also just a tragic accident, not a curse.

title: The government has changed the Roswell story FOUR TIMES since 1947. Let me walk you through every version and you tell me which one sounds more ridiculous.
content:
Let's play a game. I'll list every official explanation the U.S. government has given for what crashed at Roswell, and you tell me if this sounds like an organization that's telling the truth.

Version 1 (July 8, 1947): The Army issues a press release saying they recovered a 'flying disc.' Their words. Not mine. Not some conspiracy website. The ACTUAL UNITED STATES MILITARY said they found a flying disc.

Version 2 (July 9, 1947): ONE DAY LATER, they change the story. Now it's a weather balloon. They hold a press conference with balloon debris that looks nothing like what the witnesses described. General Ramey literally posed for photos with substitute materials.

Version 3 (1994): After 47 years of 'weather balloon,' the Air Force suddenly says actually it was a Project Mogul balloon. A classified nuclear detection balloon. Oh so it WASN'T a weather balloon? So you lied for 47 years? Cool cool cool.

Version 4 (1997): The Air Force publishes ANOTHER report to explain the 'alien bodies' witnesses reported. Their explanation? Crash test dummies dropped from high altitude in the 1950s. Except the Roswell crash was in 1947. The dummy drops started in 1953. SIX YEARS LATER. The Air Force's official explanation is that witnesses confused events from different DECADES. That's their story.

Now let's look at what the witnesses actually said. Jesse Marcel, the intelligence officer who first examined the debris, went to his grave saying it was not from any balloon. Multiple witnesses described metallic material that couldn't be bent, cut, or burned. Brazel's son said the debris had properties unlike anything he'd ever seen.

Four stories in 50 years. Each one contradicting the last. And somehow I'M the crazy one for asking questions. They don't want you thinking about this. They want you to accept Version 4 and move on. But if they've lied three times already, why would the fourth time be the truth?

Connect the dots. Or don't. They're counting on you not to.

title: The 9/11 Commission Report is 585 pages and publicly available — here's what people always get wrong about it
content:
I finally sat down and read big chunks of the 9/11 Commission Report after years of hearing people argue about what it does and doesn't say. It's actually surprisingly readable for a government document. And a lot of the common claims about it online are just... wrong.

The attacks were planned and carried out by al-Qaeda, led by Osama bin Laden. 19 hijackers took over four commercial aircraft on September 11, 2001. 15 of the 19 hijackers were Saudi nationals, which is a real and important detail that has led to legitimate ongoing investigations into whether Saudi officials had any involvement. The Commission itself said it found no evidence the Saudi government as an institution funded the attacks, but also noted that Saudi charities and individuals may have been funding sources — which is a pretty important distinction.

What blew my mind was the operational detail. The plot took years to develop. Bin Laden initially wanted to hit nuclear power plants but was talked out of it. The hijackers lived in the US for months, some for over a year, taking flying lessons and blending in. The report is also brutally honest about intelligence failures — the CIA and FBI had pieces of the puzzle but didn't share information. There were multiple missed opportunities to disrupt the plot.

The engineering analysis of the tower collapses is also fascinating and heartbreaking. The NIST investigation found that the jet fuel fires weakened the steel floor trusses until they sagged and pulled the exterior columns inward, leading to progressive collapse. It wasn't an explosion — it was a structural failure under extraordinary conditions that no building had ever been designed to withstand.

Genuinely recommend reading at least the executive summary. It's one of those things where the actual facts are more compelling — and more disturbing — than any alternative theory.

title: TIL the German city of Bielefeld has been the subject of a 30-year satirical conspiracy theory that it doesn't exist
content:
Ok so this is genuinely one of my favorite pieces of internet history. In 1994, a German computer science student named Achim Held posted a tongue-in-cheek message to Usenet (basically prehistoric Reddit) claiming that the city of Bielefeld doesn't actually exist. He laid out three questions: Do you know anyone from Bielefeld? Have you ever been to Bielefeld? Do you know anyone who has been to Bielefeld? And for most Germans, the answer to all three was... no.

The joke absolutely exploded. It became THE meme of German internet culture before memes were even a thing. The running gag is that Bielefeld is a fabrication by 'THEM' (never specified who) and any evidence of Bielefeld's existence is part of the cover-up. If you say you've been there, you're in on it. If you show a map with Bielefeld on it, the map was doctored.

The best part? Bielefeld is a totally real city with over 330,000 people. It's in North Rhine-Westphalia, has a university, a castle from the 13th century, and is a major hub for the food processing industry. Even Angela Merkel once joked about it at a press conference in 2012, saying 'if it exists at all' and then had to clarify she was joking after it went viral.

In 2019, Bielefeld's city marketing department offered a million euros to anyone who could definitively prove the city doesn't exist. They got over 2,000 submissions. Nobody won obviously, but the marketing campaign was genius.

It's basically proof that if you commit to a bit hard enough for three decades, it becomes cultural heritage.

title: There's a reason the US Navy tested their most classified underwater sonar systems in the Bermuda Triangle and nobody talks about it
content:
Everyone wants to "debunk" the Bermuda Triangle by saying it's just a busy shipping lane. Cool. Explain Flight 19. Five planes, fourteen men, vanished. The RESCUE plane they sent to find them? Also vanished. The Navy's official report literally listed the cause as "reasons unknown." Not weather. Not pilot error. REASONS. UNKNOWN. The Navy doesn't write that on an official report unless they're covering something.

And it's not just Flight 19. The USS Cyclops in 1918 — 309 crew, largest non-combat loss of life in US Navy history — gone. No distress signal. No wreckage. No bodies. NOTHING. And then BOTH of its sister ships disappeared in the same area during WWII. Three identical ships, same area, all gone without a trace. Statistically that's basically impossible.

Here's what nobody wants to connect: the Bermuda Triangle sits directly above the deepest point in the entire Atlantic Ocean — the Puerto Rico Trench, nearly 28,000 feet deep. We have better maps of Mars than we do of that trench. What's down there? We literally don't know. And every time someone tries to do deep exploration there, equipment "malfunctions."

Columbus himself wrote in his log about seeing strange lights under the water and his compass going haywire in this exact area. IN 1492. Before engines, before fuel, before any of the "rational explanations" people use today.

But sure, it's just "busy shipping lanes" and "confirmation bias." The insurance companies and debunkers have it all figured out. Nothing to see here. Move along. Don't look at the ocean. Definitely don't look at what AUTEC is doing on Andros Island. That's just a normal Navy testing facility. In the middle of the Triangle. For acoustics. Sure.

Wake up.

title: TIL Loch Ness has been extensively studied and the actual biology of the lake is way more interesting than a monster
content:
Ok so I went to Scotland last month and obviously had to visit Loch Ness. I ended up spending like 3 hours at the Loch Ness Centre reading about all the actual scientific surveys that have been done and honestly the real science is way cooler than Nessie.

First off, Loch Ness is genuinely massive and kind of terrifying on its own. It's the largest body of freshwater in the UK by volume — it contains more water than all the lakes in England and Wales COMBINED. It's 230 meters deep in places and the water is so dark with peat that visibility is basically zero past a few feet. So I get why people's imaginations go wild.

In 2019, a team from New Zealand did a comprehensive environmental DNA (eDNA) survey of the entire loch. Basically, every living thing sheds DNA into the water through skin cells, waste, etc. You can filter the water and sequence everything living in it. They found no DNA from large unknown species. No plesiosaur DNA. No large reptile DNA of any kind. What they DID find was a massive amount of European eel DNA — way more than expected.

The leading scientific theory now is that Loch Ness may contain some unusually large eels. European eels can grow pretty big in the right conditions, and the loch's deep, cold, peat-dark water could potentially allow eels to grow larger than normal. A 4-6 foot eel surfacing in dark water could absolutely look like a "monster" to someone on shore, especially in poor light.

The lake also has healthy populations of Atlantic salmon, brown trout, Arctic char, and pike. The pike can get pretty big too — up to a meter long. Any of these could create weird shapes at the surface.

The most famous photo — the "Surgeon's Photo" from 1934 — was confirmed as a hoax in 1994. It was a toy submarine with a sculpted head attached. The guy who helped build it confessed on his deathbed.

But here's the thing I actually love: even knowing all this, standing at the edge of that loch in the fog, with the dark water stretching out farther than you can see... your brain WANTS there to be something in there. It's such a perfectly eerie place. I totally understand why the legend has persisted for centuries. The loch itself is the real monster tbh.

title: Why do so many conspiracy myths cluster around aviation and the Cold War?
content:
I’m noticing a pattern: so many sticky conspiracies center on aircraft, space/defense tech, and Cold War incidents (Area 51, Roswell, KAL 007, black helicopters, Bermuda Triangle, etc.).

Genuine question: what makes these domains such fertile ground for myths?

- Is it secrecy + plausible deniability (classified programs, delayed declassifications)?
- Sensory ambiguity (high-altitude optics, radar oddities, human perception limits)?
- Media incentives — spectacular narratives outcompete mundane explanations?
- Cold War institutional behaviors (cover stories that unintentionally fuel speculation)?
- Psychological appeal — agency, threat, pattern-finding in sparse data?

If you’ve got citations, declassified docs, or case studies (e.g., U-2/SR-71 misreports, Project Mogul, AATIP framing), I’d love to dig in. Also curious about non-aviation analogs (e.g., undersea cables/submarines) and whether similar dynamics apply.

title: TIL in 2012 CERN actually discovered the Higgs boson and it's way cooler than people realize
content:
So I was going down a rabbit hole about particle physics last night and honestly the Higgs boson discovery is one of the most underrated things that happened in 2012. Like, scientists spent 50 years and billions of dollars building the largest machine ever constructed by humans, just to find a particle that exists for a fraction of a fraction of a second. And they actually found it.

Peter Higgs literally cried at the announcement. This dude theorized about this particle in 1964 and had to wait almost half a century to see if he was right. Imagine writing a paper and then waiting 48 years for someone to check your homework.

The LHC smashes protons together at nearly the speed of light, and they had to sift through petabytes of data to find the signal. It's like finding a specific grain of sand on every beach on Earth simultaneously. The engineering alone is insane — the magnets inside the LHC are colder than outer space.

But sure, people on the internet decided it was about black holes lmao.

title: Proposal: A simple ‘Claim → Cite’ checklist for myth-busting posts
content:
If we want better signal on myth vs. reality, let’s standardize how we cite. Draft checklist below — feedback welcome.

Claim → Cite checklist (v0.1)
- Primary sources first: official docs, datasets, agency reports (e.g., NTSB/FAA, DoD releases, court filings).
- Data link: if you mention stats or risk, link the dataset or a neutral aggregator (Lloyd’s, NOAA, NCEI).
- Date + scope: note timeframes, definitions, and what the claim specifically excludes.
- Contradictory evidence: acknowledge reputable counterpoints and why they don’t overturn the main claim.
- Uncertainty: state what’s unknown and avoid overreach.
- Archival: include a web archive link (Wayback/Perma) for key sources to prevent link-rot.

If there’s interest, I’ll turn this into a reusable template we can paste at the bottom of debunks. Add what you’d want to see!

title: TIL 'black helicopters' are just regular government helicopters and the reason they're black is incredibly boring
content:
So I went down this rabbit hole after someone at work mentioned "black helicopters" in a joking conspiracy theory way and I realized I had no idea what the actual story was. Turns out it's one of the most hilariously mundane explanations ever.

Black helicopters are just... helicopters that are painted black. That's it. U.S. Customs and Border Protection uses them for patrol. The military uses them for special operations and combat search and rescue. Various law enforcement agencies use dark-colored helicopters because — and I cannot stress this enough — black paint exists and someone had to pick a color.

The conspiracy theory really took off in the 1990s when militia groups and far-right organizations started claiming that unmarked black helicopters were part of a UN plot to invade America or some kind of New World Order surveillance program. In reality, military helicopters are often painted dark for pretty obvious tactical reasons (harder to see at night), and many don't have visible markings because that's just standard military practice.

What makes this funny is that the helicopters were never even secret. The US Army's 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment literally goes by the nickname "Night Stalkers" and they fly — you guessed it — black helicopters. It's not classified. They have a Wikipedia page. They have a motto. They have challenge coins you can buy on eBay.

The whole "black helicopters" thing has become such a cultural meme that it's now shorthand for any conspiracy theory involving government surveillance. Which is ironic because the actual surveillance they should worry about is happening through their phones, not helicopters.

title: TIL a cold snap doesn't disprove global warming and the science behind why is actually fascinating
content:
Every winter without fail, some uncle on Facebook posts a picture of snow and writes "so much for global warming LOL." And every year I die a little inside. So I finally went deep on this topic and honestly the actual science is way more interesting than the gotcha.

Weather and climate are fundamentally different things. Weather is what's happening outside your window right now. Climate is the pattern over decades. Saying "it's cold today so global warming is fake" is like saying "I ate lunch today so world hunger is solved." One data point tells you nothing about a 30-year trend.

But here's where it gets really cool (pun intended): global warming can actually CAUSE more extreme cold snaps. The polar vortex — this band of cold air that normally sits tight around the Arctic — is held in place by the jet stream. As the Arctic warms faster than everywhere else (it's warming about 4x faster than the global average), the temperature difference that powers the jet stream weakens. When the jet stream weakens, it gets wobbly, and chunks of polar air spill way further south than they normally would. That's why Texas got that insane freeze in 2021.

So paradoxically, some of the most brutal cold events we've seen recently are actually consistent with a warming planet. The overall global average temperature keeps climbing — 2023 and 2024 were the hottest years ever recorded — but the distribution of temperature extremes gets weirder.

Climate science is one of those things where the more you learn, the more you realize the "common sense" objections are just people not understanding the difference between a snapshot and a trend. Not trying to be preachy, I just think the polar vortex thing is genuinely mind-blowing.

title: TIL Barack Obama was born at Kapiolani Medical Center in Honolulu, Hawaii, and the birth certificate saga is one of the wildest political episodes in modern US history
content:
I've been reading about the 2008-2012 political era and honestly the birther thing is absolutely wild in hindsight. So here's the actual facts:

Barack Obama was born on August 4, 1961, at Kapiolani Medical Center for Women and Children in Honolulu, Hawaii. Hawaii became a U.S. state on August 21, 1959 — two full years before Obama was born. He was born in America. That's it. That's the story.

But the conspiracy got so out of hand that Obama became the first (and only) president in U.S. history to publicly release his long-form birth certificate, which he did in April 2011. The Hawaii Department of Health confirmed it. The state's Republican governor at the time confirmed it. Two Honolulu newspapers published birth announcements in August 1961. His birth was announced in BOTH the Honolulu Advertiser and the Honolulu Star-Bulletin. In 1961. Before he was a politician. Before he was anything.

The conspiracy theory implied that somehow, in 1961, someone planted fake birth announcements in two separate newspapers for a random baby, anticipating that this kid would one day run for president. That is genuinely the logical conclusion you have to reach for the theory to work.

Also, fun fact that most people don't know: even if Obama HAD been born abroad, he still would have been a natural-born U.S. citizen because his mother, Ann Dunham, was an American citizen. The same way Ted Cruz was born in Canada and John McCain was born in Panama, and both ran for president without legal challenges to their eligibility.

The whole thing was studied by FactCheck.org, PolitiFact, and basically every major news organization. All confirmed: born in Hawaii. It's genuinely not even a close call.

title: TIL the Roswell 'UFO crash' was actually a top-secret nuclear surveillance balloon from Project Mogul, and the government covered it up — but not for the reason you think
content:
Ok so the Roswell story is way more interesting when you know what actually happened, because there WAS a cover-up. Just not the alien kind.

In June 1947, a rancher named Mac Brazel found weird debris scattered across his property near Roswell, New Mexico. Tinfoil, rubber strips, sticks, metallic-looking tape with strange symbols on it. He called the local sheriff, who called Roswell Army Air Field. A public information officer named Walter Haut issued a press release saying they'd recovered a 'flying disc.' This was 1947 — everyone was seeing flying saucers. The press went insane.

The very next day, the military retracted the statement and said it was a weather balloon. Case closed. Except it wasn't a weather balloon either.

It was actually a balloon array from Project Mogul — a classified program designed to detect Soviet nuclear tests using high-altitude acoustic sensors. The Cold War had just started. The Soviets were racing to build nuclear weapons. The U.S. needed to know when they tested one. So they launched these massive balloon trains (we're talking 600+ feet of gear) carrying microphones into the upper atmosphere to listen for the sound signatures of nuclear detonations.

The weird symbols on the tape? They were from a novelty toy manufacturer that made the reinforcing tape for the balloon targets. Literally just decorative tape from a kids' toy company. The metallic material was radar reflectors.

The military couldn't say 'nuclear surveillance balloon' because the program was classified. So they said weather balloon, which sounded suspicious, which made everyone think aliens, which honestly was probably preferable to the Soviets finding out about Mogul. The real cover-up was hiding Cold War spy tech, not alien bodies.

This was all declassified in the 1990s. The Air Force published two massive reports in 1994 and 1997 explaining everything. But by then the alien story was a multi-billion dollar tourism industry for Roswell, so, you know. The truth had some competition.

title: TIL Korean Air Lines Flight 007 was shot down by a Soviet fighter jet in 1983 because of a navigation error, and the full story is a Cold War nightmare
content:
I just spent an entire evening reading about KAL 007 and I am genuinely shaken. This story has everything — Cold War paranoia, a catastrophic navigation mistake, 269 dead civilians, and it almost started World War III.

On September 1, 1983, Korean Air Lines Flight 007 was flying from New York to Seoul via Anchorage, Alaska. Somewhere after the Anchorage refueling stop, the plane drifted off course and flew into Soviet prohibited airspace over the Kamchatka Peninsula and Sakhalin Island. The Soviets scrambled fighter jets, and a Su-15 interceptor fired two air-to-air missiles. The plane went down in the Sea of Japan. All 269 people on board were killed, including a sitting U.S. congressman, Larry McDonald.

The most likely cause of the deviation was a navigation error. The crew probably failed to properly set the autopilot from heading mode to INS (inertial navigation system) mode after departing Anchorage. This meant the plane flew on a constant magnetic heading instead of following the planned route, which caused it to gradually drift hundreds of miles off course over several hours. A tiny cockpit mistake with apocalyptic consequences.

The Soviet pilot, Major Gennadi Osipovich, later said he fired warning shots with tracer rounds and tried to make radio contact, but KAL 007 didn't respond. The Soviets genuinely believed it was a U.S. spy plane — an RC-135 reconnaissance aircraft had been operating in the same area that night, and the two aircraft's radar signatures may have been confused.

The incident was a massive diplomatic crisis. Reagan called it a "massacre" and used it to justify the Strategic Defense Initiative. The Soviets initially denied shooting it down, then claimed it was a deliberate spy mission. It took years for the full picture to emerge. The black box was recovered by the Soviets but kept secret until 1992.

One positive outcome: the incident led Reagan to make GPS technology available to civilians, specifically so commercial aircraft would never have this kind of navigation error again. Every time you use GPS on your phone, it traces back to 269 people who died because a pilot set his autopilot wrong.

title: Why did Disney's family hold the funeral in SECRET and cremate him within 48 hours? Because they had to hide the body. Here's why.
content:
Let me walk you through the timeline because nobody ever does.

December 15, 1966: Walt Disney dies. December 17: Cremated. No public funeral. No open casket. No viewing. The family says nothing until it's already done. 48 hours. That's it. The most famous man in American entertainment and they speedran his funeral like they were hiding evidence.

Now the official story is that his ashes are at Forest Lawn Memorial Park. Sure. But here's what they don't want you to think about: the first cryogenic preservation of a human happened ONE MONTH later, in January 1967. James Bedford. And guess where the Cryonics Society of California was based? GLENDALE. The same city as Forest Lawn. You cannot make this up.

Disney was obsessed with the future. He literally built EPCOT as a prototype city of tomorrow. He spent his last years planning a utopian community. This was a man who wanted to live forever. And you're telling me he heard about cryonics and said 'nah, just burn me'?

And let's talk about the Pirates of the Caribbean ride. It opened in 1967, just months after Disney's death. It was the last ride he personally supervised. There's a hidden underground complex beneath the ride that they call 'Utilidors' — maintenance tunnels. Sure. 'Maintenance.' Has anyone actually verified what's in all of those tunnels? Has anyone done a full thermal scan of the underground areas at Disneyland?

I'm not saying Walt Disney is frozen under Pirates of the Caribbean. I'm saying nobody has PROVEN he isn't. And in a park built by a man who literally made dreams come true, you'd think people would be a little more open-minded.

But sure. Cremated in 48 hours. Nothing to see here. Move along.

title: TIL the 'Ted Cruz is the Zodiac Killer' meme started as a joke in 2013 and then 38% of Florida voters said they weren't sure it was false
content:
Ok so I just went down the funniest Wikipedia rabbit hole. The whole "Ted Cruz is the Zodiac Killer" thing started as a Twitter joke around 2013 and somehow became one of the most persistent political memes of the decade. The best part? Ted Cruz was born in 1970 in Calgary, Canada. The Zodiac Killer was active in Northern California in the late 1960s. Cruz was literally a baby. In a different country.

But here's where it gets actually hilarious — Public Policy Polling did a survey in 2016 and found that 38% of Florida voters said they were "not sure" whether Ted Cruz was the Zodiac Killer. Not that they believed it — they just couldn't rule it out. For a crime that happened before he was born. In another country.

The real Zodiac Killer was never caught, which is genuinely one of the most fascinating unsolved cases in American history. He operated in the San Francisco Bay Area in the late '60s and early '70s, sent coded letters to newspapers, and at least four of his ciphers were never solved. The FBI officially kept the case open until 2004, and amateur codebreakers are still working on the remaining ciphers.

Cruz himself eventually leaned into the meme. He tweeted a Zodiac-related joke on Halloween 2018, which honestly is probably the most likable thing he's ever done regardless of your politics. His communications team clearly decided "if you can't beat 'em, join 'em."

The internet is truly an incredible place where you can accuse a sitting senator of being a serial killer from before he was born and nearly 4 in 10 people will go "well, I mean, I guess I can't prove he WASN'T."

title: Avril Lavigne's handwriting, voice, face shape, and birthmarks ALL changed after 2003. This is the one conspiracy I can't debunk.
content:
I'm not a conspiracy person. I think the moon landing was real, I think the earth is round, I think vaccines work. But the Avril Lavigne thing keeps me up at night because I genuinely cannot explain it away.

The music label hired a lookalike named Melissa Vandella in 2002 to serve as a decoy for paparazzi. This isn't disputed. There are photos of them together. The label admitted to using decoys. So the replacement already existed.

Now compare Sk8er Boi era Avril to post-2004 Avril side by side. The nose is different. The jawline is different. She went from being 5'1" to appearing noticeably taller. Her birthmark on her right arm? Gone. Just... gone. People say makeup. Sure. On every single appearance for twenty years. Never once forgetting.

Her handwriting changed completely. There are signed albums from 2002 and signed albums from 2005 and the handwriting analysis doesn't match. Her vocal range shifted. Her songwriting style underwent not an evolution but a complete discontinuity — there's a reason Under My Skin sounds like a different artist wrote it. Because one did.

And the kicker — she was photographed with "Melissa" written on her hand. People say a fan wrote it. Show me the fan. Name the fan. Nobody can. Because it was a slip-up. A moment where she forgot who she was supposed to be.

Her close friends and collaborators from the Let Go era all stopped working with her after 2003. Every single one. Her relationship with her family visibly changed. Old friends gave interviews saying she "wasn't the same person" and everyone just assumed they meant it figuratively.

I don't WANT this to be true. But I've spent 200+ hours on this and I can't debunk it. If you can, I'm genuinely all ears.

title: Former Area 51 employees keep dying before their interviews and nobody wants to talk about the pattern
content:
Let's start with what the government has actually ADMITTED. They lied about Area 51 existing for 58 years. Not speculated about, not kinda-sorta denied — they actively, deliberately lied about the existence of an entire military base for over half a century. They finally admitted it in 2013. So when people say "the government wouldn't lie about something that big" — yes they would, and they did. For 58 years. About a base you can SEE ON GOOGLE MAPS.

Now let's talk about Bob Lazar. In 1989 he went on TV and said he worked at S-4, a facility near Area 51, reverse-engineering alien spacecraft. He described the propulsion system, Element 115, the layout of the facility. Everyone called him crazy. Then in 2003, scientists synthesized Element 115 (Moscovium) and it behaves suspiciously close to how he described. Lucky guess? From a guy who also correctly described the hand-bone scanner at the facility years before one was publicly known to exist there?

The government's response to Lazar was interesting. They didn't say "he's wrong." They said "he never worked here." They scrubbed his employment records, his MIT records, his Los Alamos records. A reporter later found his name in a Los Alamos phone directory. Whoops.

In 2017 the Pentagon admitted they ran a secret UFO investigation program called AATIP. In 2020 they released Navy pilot videos of objects performing maneuvers that break known physics — instantaneous acceleration, transmedium travel, no visible propulsion. The Pentagon confirmed the videos are real and the objects are "unidentified." They created a whole new office for it.

So let me get this straight: the government lied about the base for 58 years, admitted they secretly studied UFOs, confirmed Navy footage of physics-defying craft, and your position is still "it's just a normal air base"?

I'm not saying it's aliens. I'm saying the government has given us every reason to believe they're hiding something extraordinary, and the fact that the best explanation they can offer for their own Navy footage is "we don't know what those are" should terrify you either way. Do your own research.

title: TIL the 'Bowling Green Massacre' never happened — the real story is actually a mundane FBI arrest from 2011
content:
Ok so you probably remember the phrase "Bowling Green Massacre" from that Kellyanne Conway interview in 2017 where she cited it as justification for a travel ban. I always assumed there was SOME kernel of truth to it that she just exaggerated. Nope. There was no massacre. Not even close.

What actually happened in Bowling Green, Kentucky in 2011 was that two Iraqi refugees — Waad Ramadan Alwan and Mohanad Shareef Hammadi — were arrested by the FBI after a sting operation. They had been trying to send money and weapons to al-Qaeda back in Iraq. Importantly: no attack was carried out, no one was hurt, and it was a standard federal law enforcement operation. They were caught, charged, and convicted. The system worked exactly as intended.

But somehow in 2017, this arrest got turned into a "massacre" on live television, and because the internet is the internet, it became a meme instantly. People started making "Never Forget" t-shirts and someone set up a GoFundMe for "survivors." The Wikipedia article for "Bowling Green massacre" literally just says it's a fictitious event.

The whole thing is actually a really interesting case study in how misinformation works. A real but relatively minor event gets inflated into something catastrophic, people who only half-heard the original claim remember the inflated version, and suddenly a bunch of people genuinely believe there was a terrorist attack in Kentucky. Brains are weird, man.

Anyway, Bowling Green is actually a nice little city. Home of the Corvette Museum. They deserve better than being famous for something that literally didn't happen.

title: Area 51's actual history is way more interesting than aliens — the real planes they tested there were basically UFOs anyway
content:
I've been on a massive Cold War aviation rabbit hole and the real story of Area 51 is honestly more fascinating than any alien theory. Buckle up.

Area 51 is officially called Groom Lake, and it's a detachment of Edwards Air Force Base in the middle of the Nevada desert. The CIA set it up in 1955 for one specific reason: to test the U-2 spy plane away from prying eyes. The U-2 could fly at 70,000 feet — way higher than anything else at the time — and the CIA needed somewhere so remote that nobody would accidentally see it during test flights.

Here's where it gets fun. The U-2 flew so high that commercial pilots and people on the ground had never seen anything at that altitude before. The sun would reflect off the silver fuselage at angles that made it look like a glowing disc in the sky. Air Force investigators literally documented that MORE THAN HALF of all UFO reports in the late 1950s were actually U-2 sightings. The Air Force couldn't explain what people were seeing because the U-2 was classified, so they just let people think it was UFOs. The government actively chose "aliens" as the better cover story over revealing their spy plane. That's incredible.

Then came the A-12 OXCART and later the SR-71 Blackbird — Mach 3+ aircraft that looked like something from a sci-fi movie. Developed and tested at Area 51. The F-117 stealth fighter, the first true stealth aircraft, was also tested there in the early 80s. When people saw this angular black triangle flying silently at night... yeah. More UFO reports.

The government didn't even officially acknowledge Area 51 existed until 2013 when the CIA declassified a bunch of U-2 program documents. Fifty-eight years of "this place doesn't exist" when you could literally see it on satellite images. Classic government moment.

So basically Area 51 IS where secret advanced aircraft are developed and tested. It's just that the aircraft are human-made. They're just so far ahead of their time that people literally thought they were alien technology. Which honestly? Might be the best compliment Lockheed's Skunk Works division has ever received.

title: TIL the Bermuda Triangle isn't actually statistically more dangerous than any other part of the ocean and the whole legend is basically manufactured
content:
So I spent way too long reading about this because a coworker was dead serious about the Bermuda Triangle being a portal or whatever, and I wanted to come with receipts.

Turns out, when you actually look at the data, the Bermuda Triangle (roughly between Miami, Bermuda, and Puerto Rico) doesn't have a higher rate of disappearances than any comparable stretch of ocean. Lloyd's of London, the world's biggest maritime insurance market, has publicly stated that the area is not especially dangerous. Insurance premiums aren't higher for ships traveling through it. If insurance companies — who literally make money by correctly assessing risk — don't think it's special, that tells you everything.

The legend basically started with a 1964 magazine article and then got supercharged by Charles Berlitz's 1974 bestseller. Researchers later found that Berlitz (and others) exaggerated cases, ignored natural explanations, and sometimes flat-out made up details. Some of the "mysterious disappearances" actually happened hundreds of miles outside the Triangle. Some of the ships had perfectly well-documented explanations like hurricanes or mechanical failure.

The area IS heavily trafficked — it's one of the busiest shipping corridors in the world — so naturally more incidents happen there in absolute numbers. It's also prone to sudden storms, the Gulf Stream can quickly erase evidence of disasters, and the Puerto Rico Trench is the deepest point in the Atlantic so wreckage may never be found.

Even Flight 19, the most famous case, was a group of trainee pilots led by a lieutenant who got disoriented, overruled his students who wanted to fly west, and flew east into open ocean until they ran out of fuel. Tragic, but not mysterious.

The Bermuda Triangle is basically what happens when confirmation bias meets good marketing.

title: TIL Walt Disney was cremated two days after his death and his ashes are in a garden at Forest Lawn cemetery — the frozen body thing is a complete myth
content:
I always assumed the whole 'Walt Disney is frozen under Disneyland' thing was at least partially true. Like maybe he was cryogenically preserved somewhere. Nope. Not even close.

Walt Disney died on December 15, 1966, from lung cancer. He was cremated on December 17, just two days later. His ashes were interred at Forest Lawn Memorial Park in Glendale, California. You can literally go visit. It's in the Freedom Mausoleum in a garden called the Court of Freedom. There are public records. There's a death certificate. The family confirmed it. Multiple biographers have documented it.

The cryonics rumor seems to have started shortly after his death, partly because the first known human to be cryogenically preserved — a psychology professor named James Bedford — was frozen in January 1967, just one month after Disney died. The timing was coincidental but people ran with it.

The irony is that cryonics was barely even a concept when Disney died. The Cryonics Society of California only formed in 1966. The idea that Disney somehow arranged this cutting-edge procedure in secret while dying of cancer is... a lot.

Also, his family was very private about the funeral. It was a small service with no public announcement until after the cremation. That secrecy probably fueled the rumors more than anything. Turns out when you don't let people see what happened, they'll make up something way more interesting.

Anyway, if you're at Forest Lawn, his spot is actually really peaceful. Just don't tell people on the internet that you went or they'll tell you the real body is under Space Mountain.

title: TIL MIT did an actual scientific study on tin foil hats in 2005 and found they AMPLIFY certain radio frequencies instead of blocking them
content:
This is one of my favorite pieces of scientific literature ever. In 2005, a group of MIT grad students published a paper called "On the Effectiveness of Aluminium Foil Helmets: An Empirical Study." They built three different helmet designs out of aluminum foil, put them on human subjects, and measured the radio frequency attenuation using a network analyzer.

The results are incredible. The helmets DID attenuate (reduce) signals across most of the tested spectrum. BUT — and this is the beautiful part — they actually AMPLIFIED signals at certain frequencies, specifically around 1.2 GHz and 2.6 GHz. The 1.2 GHz range is allocated for aeronautical radionavigation and space-to-Earth satellite communication. So if the government WERE beaming signals at you from a satellite, a tin foil hat would literally make the reception better. Chef's kiss.

The whole concept goes back way further than I thought, too. The first mention of a tin foil hat as mind-control protection is from a 1927 science fiction story called "The Tissue-Culture King" by Julian Huxley (brother of Aldous Huxley, the Brave New World guy). In the story, the protagonist uses a hat made of metal foil to shield himself from telepathic mind control. So the entire idea literally comes from fiction.

From a physics standpoint, a Faraday cage (which is what a foil hat is trying to be) needs to fully enclose the object being shielded and be properly grounded to work. A hat that's open at the bottom and not grounded is basically just a crinkly fashion statement. Your microwave oven is a better Faraday cage than a tin foil hat.

Anyway, if you're going to go through the trouble, at least wrap your entire head. And ground yourself. The MIT paper is free online and it's a genuinely fun 5-minute read.
